overview: Gunaikurnai communities connect Gippsland Country with clan identities, stories and responsibilities. Public community institutions sustain living knowledge while acknowledging diverse family and local traditions.

items.text: GLaWAC recognises five major clans. It explains Gunaikurnai as the agreed combined name acknowledging recorded forms Gunnai and Kurnai and their descendants.
The Knob on Brayakaulung Country served as a gathering place where clans shared news, traded goods, feasted and practised ceremonies.
The Dooyeedang, or Avon River, connected the high country and Gippsland Lakes as a travelling route and supplied foods including eels and fish.
Grinding grooves beneath the bluff at the Knob record the sharpening of stone axe heads on sandstone. Camps and scarred trees also survive in the landscape.
Gunaikurnai cultural fire connects care for land with ceremony and communication. Elders and knowledge holders guide its renewal in appropriate places and seasons.
People continued meeting at the Knob during the mission era, maintaining family connections despite separation. The site hosted the 2010 native title determination ceremony.
The Cultural Hub at Forestec provides community programmes that support traditional knowledge, values and cultural learning. Stories and songlines remain connected to Country and ancestors.
